keep: The idea is named up front: a big start dips the voltage before the AVR can act, the engine deepens it, the AVR and governor pull it back, and the cures all cut the starting kVA each set carries.

The first dip is caused, not asserted: only the sub-transient reactance (0.15, as for fault currents) holds the current back, and it shares the voltage with the motor's starting impedance like a divider: 630 / 600 = 1.05 pu, 1.05 / 1.20 = 87.5%. Labelled a simplified picture.

Recovery has its own cause: after the first cycles Xs = 1.5 carries the current and the AVR's field has a ceiling (example E 2.5), so 600 kVA recovers to 100% but 900 kVA only to 2.5 / (1 + 1.5 x 900/630) = 79.5% and stalls. The picture shows both sides of the rule (gets away and stalls).
Every figure answer is typed with slips: 600 A recall, 82.4%, 72.3% torque, 93.3% star-delta, 90.3% with a second set, 240 kW. Options only for the AVR prediction and the governor-fails-high puzzle.
Both misconceptions in the brief have a DO screen: the AVR prevents the dip (screen 3, prediction before the start, [^2]) and a change at one set stays there (screen 13).
Thirteen screens alternate DO 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 with SHOW 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ending on three mixed puzzles (11 synchronise a second set first, 12 kW against kVA, 13 one governor fails high).

The sub-main analogy reproduces the main result (source impedance and starting impedance share the voltage; a bigger cable, a parallel feed or a soft start shrink the dip); its breaks name the reactance growing from sub-transient to synchronous and the missing frequency dip.
